passage:
I'm Damini, and the day the results came out was Dhanteras; our whole lane was buying steel pots and lighting diyas. I'd cleared the bank PO exam. First attempt. The thing my father had talked about since I was fourteen, the thing Eshaan and my whole coaching batch had pinned on the wall.
Everyone called. My phone was hot in my hand. Mummy made kheer. I smiled at every single person and said thank you.
And then at night, on the terrace, with the diyas burning down, I waited for the feeling. The big one. It never came. It was just quiet. Like finishing someone else's homework.
Eshaan messaged: "Now you're set for life!" I typed "yes!!" and put the phone face down. I kept thinking about the evenings I'd skipped pottery class at the community centre to study reasoning. I'd liked the pottery. I never told anyone that.

qa.q: Which exam had Damini cleared?
qa.a: The bank PO exam, on the first attempt.

qa.q: What did Damini feel on the terrace that night?
qa.a: Damini felt empty and flat instead of joyful, as if the win belonged to someone else, "like finishing someone else's homework".

qa.q: What could Damini do with that empty feeling?
qa.a: Treat it as information: take time to ask what Damini actually values, perhaps go back to pottery, and talk honestly at home about what comes next instead of just typing "yes!!".

qa.q: How might Damini's father see the result?
qa.a: Damini's father has talked about it since Damini was fourteen, so the father probably feels proud and relieved, with no idea of the emptiness behind the smiles.

grounding: A young adult reaches a goal set by family and friends and feels empty, because it never matched the narrator's own interests.

During the summer holidays the power went off every afternoon in Urmila's building in Hyderabad, and the children gathered in Irfan's flat, where the windows caught a breeze. Irfan's father had brought a box of new puzzles: a wooden cube, a metal ring puzzle, a tangram set.
Irfan dived for the cube. Urmila went to the shelf and took down the jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.
"Try the rings," Irfan said. "Nobody knows how to do it."
"I like the parrot."
"You've done the parrot a hundred times!"
"So? I can do it." She snapped the pieces into place. When Irfan finally solved the cube and shouted, she smiled, but she didn't touch it. The ring puzzle stayed in its box all afternoon.

qa.q: Which puzzle did Urmila take down?
qa.a: The jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.

qa.q: Why does Urmila keep choosing the parrot jigsaw?
qa.a: Urmila feels safe with a puzzle she can't get wrong; the new ones might make her feel stupid, so avoiding them keeps the worry away.

qa.q: How could an adult help Urmila try something new?
qa.a: Pair her with Irfan on the ring puzzle, praise the trying rather than the solving, and show that getting stuck is part of puzzles, not a sign of being bad at them.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Urmila's choice?
qa.a: Irfan finds it puzzling and a bit frustrating that she repeats the parrot "a hundred times" while new puzzles sit waiting.

grounding: A child afraid of being wrong sticks to a jigsaw she already knows and avoids new puzzles, which feels safe but blocks learning.

The inter-school debate in Pune was held in the last week of December, with a Christmas tree still blinking in the auditorium lobby. Vaibhav had prepared for three weeks. In the final round he blanked on his rebuttal, stood silent for ten long seconds, and his team lost by two points.
In January, Hafsa pinned the next notice on the class board. "Youth parliament, February. You're coming, right? You're our best speaker."
"I'm not," Vaibhav said. "Everyone saw what I am."
"You froze once."
"In front of the whole school." He didn't look at the notice. At lunch he sat away from the debate group, and when the teacher asked who wanted to open the class discussion, he kept his eyes on his notebook.
That night he deleted the debate folder from his laptop, then restored it, then shut the laptop.

qa.q: How long did Vaibhav stand silent in the final round?
qa.a: Ten long seconds.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav say "Everyone saw what I am"?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels ashamed; to him the frozen rebuttal is not a bad moment but proof about his worth, so another contest feels like risking more humiliation.

qa.q: What could help Vaibhav return to debating?
qa.a: Separating the task from his worth: going over what went wrong with a teacher, practising rebuttals where little is at stake, and perhaps taking a smaller role in February.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Vaibhav?
qa.a: Hafsa still sees him as "our best speaker" who froze once, not someone defined by one loss, and wants him back on the team.

grounding: A teenager who froze and lost a debate feels his worth has dropped and avoids the next contest.

12 January, Lohri night

The bonfire on the terrace is still going, and I'm writing by its light because I don't want to go down yet.
Elective registration closed at 5 pm today. I picked Business Communication. Again. Easy A, everybody says. Eshaan picked astronomy, the one with the telescope nights and the terrifying maths, and asked, "Aren't you coming? You've been talking about stars since school."
I said I couldn't risk my CGPA. 9.1 is what I have. One B and it drops, and then placements, and then... I don't even know what then. I just know I can't be the one who fell.
So now I'm the one with an easy A in a class I'll forget, and Eshaan gets the telescope. The fire's sending little sparks up. I keep watching them.

Sarita

qa.q: Which elective did Sarita pick?
qa.a: Business Communication.

qa.q: Why did Sarita pick the safe elective, and how does Sarita feel about it?
qa.a: Sarita is afraid of falling short, of one B, a lower CGPA and being "the one who fell", so the safe choice feels necessary; watching the sparks, Sarita seems wistful about the astronomy Sarita loves.

qa.q: What could Sarita try before the next registration?
qa.a: Sarita could weigh what a lower grade would really cost against years of wondering, ask the astronomy teacher about maths support, or sit in on a class first.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about Sarita's choice?
qa.a: Eshaan seems disappointed and puzzled, knowing Sarita has talked about stars since school.

grounding: A student picks the easy course to protect a high grade average and never tries astronomy, letting fear of falling short make the choice.

Mentor's note: Jasleen, second meeting, community business programme.
In March, Jasleen's tiffin service closed after seven months. Today she came in with two handwritten pages titled "What the tiffin taught me". Among the lines: priced too low from day one; relied on one office for most orders; never asked customers why they stopped. She had already shown the list to her sister Rekha and to her old landlord and asked what she had missed. Rekha added one line: "You never took a day off."
She was calm, a bit tired. She said, "I cried for a week. Then I decided it was data, not a sentence."
Her new idea is a weekend baking stall. I watched her apply the list line by line: a trial month, three different buyers before growing, a short feedback card in every box.
Next step: I will review the trial-month plan with her on the 20th.

qa.q: What was the title of Jasleen's two handwritten pages?
qa.a: "What the tiffin taught me".

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel about the failure now?
qa.a: Jasleen is calm and a bit tired; after a week of crying she decided to treat it as "data, not a sentence", so she feels ready to try again.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's steps turn failure into learning?
qa.a: Writing down specific lessons, asking trusted people like Rekha what she missed, and applying each lesson to the baking plan: a trial month, several buyers and feedback cards.

qa.q: What does Rekha's added line suggest about how she saw the tiffin months?
qa.a: Rekha's "You never took a day off" suggests she worried about Jasleen wearing herself out, and sees rest as part of doing it better next time.

grounding: A mentor's note shows an adult who failed at a business writing down what she learned, sharing it with trusted people and applying it to the next attempt.

The week before Losar, Dolma's classroom in North Delhi was so cold that everyone kept their sweaters on. In science, Sudha Ma'am held up a picture. "Is a bat a bird or a mammal?"
Dolma raised her hand. "A bird—" Sudha Ma'am's eyebrows lifted slightly. "I mean, a mammal! A mammal, Ma'am."
"Why?"
Dolma looked at Ma'am's face, then at the other children's faces, searching. "Because... you said?"
"I didn't say anything yet," Sudha Ma'am said gently.
Dolma's cheeks went hot. For the next question she waited until Ma'am nodded at someone else. At lunch she told her friend she had read that bats feed their babies milk. She had known the reason all along. She just hadn't trusted it.

qa.q: What did Dolma answer first?
qa.a: "A bird."

qa.q: Why did Dolma switch her answer?
qa.a: Dolma was anxious for Ma'am's approval, and the lifted eyebrows seemed like a sign she was wrong, so she changed it to please rather than to think.

qa.q: How could Sudha Ma'am help Dolma trust her own thinking?
qa.a: Keep a neutral face, ask "How do you know?" after every answer, and praise reasons rather than right answers, so Dolma learns her own thinking counts.

qa.q: What might Sudha Ma'am notice when Dolma says "Because... you said?"
qa.a: She likely notices that Dolma is reading faces instead of thinking, which is why she gently points out she hasn't said anything yet.

grounding: A child changes her answer to whatever seems to please the teacher and searches faces for approval instead of trusting what she knows.

Diwali break, day 3

Went to Madhuri's for the card party. Seven of us.
Madhuri said the new girl, Esther, "thinks she's so smart" because she answers in class. Everyone agreed. I agreed. I actually like Esther. She lent me her notes when I was sick.
Then the joke about Esther's accent. Everyone laughed. I laughed. It wasn't even funny. My face hurt from laughing at things that weren't funny.
Madhuri asked if the movie we saw last week was boring and I said "so boring", and I LOVED that movie. I cried at the end. Why did I say that?
I think if I say one wrong thing, they'll look at each other the way they look at Esther. And then I'll be the one they talk about at the next party.
Tomorrow Esther's coming to our block for the rangoli. I don't know how to look at her.

Parveen

qa.q: What did Parveen say about last week's movie?
qa.a: "So boring", even though Parveen loved it and cried at the end.

qa.q: Why does Parveen agree and laugh against Parveen's own view?
qa.a: Parveen is afraid of rejection; one wrong word might bring the look the group gives Esther, so their approval feels more important than being honest.

qa.q: What small step could Parveen take?
qa.a: Parveen could skip laughing at the next mean joke, or quietly say "I liked the movie", and be friendly to Esther at the rangoli tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Esther feel if she heard about the party?
qa.a: Esther, who lent Parveen her notes, would likely feel hurt and betrayed to learn she was mocked, especially by someone she helped.

grounding: A teenager agrees with friends against the narrator's own view and laughs at jokes the narrator dislikes, out of fear of rejection.

passage:
Dear Irfan,
Writing from home. Navratri lights everywhere, and Mummy has asked me three times whether I'm eating properly.
I need to tell someone this. Before I buy anything, even a shirt, I send Papa a photo and wait for "Very nice, beta." Before I told my professor I'd take the research project, I called home first. When Papa said "Good choice", I felt like I could breathe.
But here's the thing. The design internship in Bengaluru, the one I actually want, they've never heard of it. Papa wants me to do government exam prep this summer, near home. Every time I think of saying no, I feel like the worst son in the world. They've given me everything.
You always seem to know what you want. How do you do it without feeling like you're betraying someone?
Darshan

qa.q: What does Darshan send Papa before buying a shirt?
qa.a: A photo, and then Darshan waits for "Very nice, beta."

qa.q: Why does Darshan feel like "the worst son in the world"?
qa.a: Darshan, a loving son, feels guilty and torn: wanting the Bengaluru internship seems like betraying parents who have given him everything.

qa.q: What could Darshan try?
qa.a: Start making small choices without checking, then talk honestly with Mummy and Papa about the internship and why it matters, instead of waiting for approval to feel allowed.

qa.q: How might Darshan's parents react if Darshan explained the internship?
qa.a: Mummy and Papa might be worried at first, wanting their son near home, but could also be proud to hear what Darshan truly wants; they cannot support a wish they have never heard.

grounding: A young man from a close family seeks his parents' praise for every choice and feels guilty that his own wish differs from theirs.

"Sonali, you're still here at nine?"
"Just finishing the Kapoor deck. And the audit notes. And Ravi's slides. He asked this afternoon."
"You said yes to Ravi too?"
"He was stuck."
"You've said yes to everyone this month. Honestly, you look wiped out."
"I'm fine. It's just... if I say no, they'll think I can't handle it."
"Nobody thinks that. Tomorrow at stand-up, when the next request comes, try: 'I can do it Thursday, not today.' I'll back you up. I'll say I need you on the client file anyway."
"You'd do that, Zubin?"
"I would. Practise on me first. I'm asking you to redo my whole budget sheet tonight."
"...I can't tonight. Thursday?"
"Perfect. Now go home."

qa.q: What was Sonali finishing at nine?
qa.a: The Kapoor deck, the audit notes and Ravi's slides.

qa.q: What seems to worry Zubin about Sonali?
qa.a: Zubin seems concerned and a little uneasy that Sonali looks wiped out and is quietly burning out from saying yes to everyone this month.

qa.q: Why is Zubin's offer a good way to help?
qa.a: It gives Sonali a concrete sentence to use, backup at stand-up so a no doesn't cost standing, and a safe practice run first.

qa.q: What is behind Sonali saying yes to everyone?
qa.a: Sonali fears that a no will make people think Sonali can't handle the work, so agreeing feels safer, even at nine at night.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate who agrees to every request and is burning out, and offers backup so the teammate can practise saying no.
